The first dot is at 42.7 GW, which is the net load in that same hour (as discussed, this is from a peak day net load reduction of 8 GW); this value is further notated with the red dashed line. As shown, there are a few hours near the far left of the figure where the net load is slightly higher than this value, this is from, for example, hours 18 and 20 in the left panel of Figure 15 where the new load is slightly higher than hour 19 (the peak hour in the baseline). But even more striking is that the hours of the year that previously had the 6000-8000th highest net load, we see even higher system net load values occurring. In total, full participation results in 24 hours of the year with higher load than the new load in the “old peak hour”, with the actual peak of the new system net load reaching 49.4 GW, which is only 2 GW lower than the baseline peak. If participation was 50% (which would still be significant) as shown in Figure 16 as yellow dots, the reduction in the old peak hour would be 4 GW, and that hour would remain as the peak. The hours with significant increases in load (on the right side of the figure) would not come close to setting new peaks. Figure 16. Net load distribution curve for the baseline system load, and the new net load in each corresponding hour after universal price response Figure 17 shows the load impact on the NEW peak net load day. In the model, this occurs in late September, when cooling loads are very large. The cooling load increases are very concentrated in the 10am-12pm window of each day, adding about 15 GW of load. But the primary reason for the new peak being set is the concentration of the EV load, which adds another 15 GW of load on the first day shown (when the new peak is set), 7 GW the following day, and only a couple of GW the third day. The EV charging model assumes all demand can be shifted over a 3-day period and can be as concentrated as the chargers’ power draw level will allow. If every single car in the state were to charge in response to the same price signal, it is reasonable to expect that the load impacts would be significant and potentially undesirable. These issues regarding highly coordinated load response will likely not matter in the near term, 31 as only a small portion of customers begin to switch to dynamic prices, and load response is limited by technology adoption and enablement, but in the long-term, strategies may be needed to avoid these impacts.
